title: The highest blessings
hookLine: the gods ask what truly brings good fortune; the first answer is about company
last: A CHILD ASLEEP ON A PARENT'S CHEST.

cards: Lucky socks on game day. Knocking on wood. Not walking under a ladder.

A lucky number on the apartment door. Every culture has its signs of good fortune, and the Buddha's India had plenty. The commentary tells a story: people argued for years about what was truly auspicious.
Was it something you see, like a bird or a pot of water? Something you hear, a good word on waking? Something you touch?
The argument spread, the story says, all the way up to the gods. So one night a god came down to the Jeta Grove to ask the Buddha.

teach.b: Mangala means blessing, good fortune, an auspicious sign. The poem is the Mangala Sutta, and it opens with the visitor's question: many gods and humans have thought about blessings, longing for well-being.
Tell us the highest. Notice what the Buddha doesn't do. He doesn't say omens are silly.
He just answers with a different kind of sign, one you can see in a life.
Not keeping company with fools. Keeping company with the wise. Honoring those who deserve honor.
That's the highest blessing, he says. That's the first verse. Your life starts with who you sit next to.

teach.h: A GOOD PLACE, LEARNING, A SKILL
teach.b: Then the next verse: living in a good place, having done good in the past, setting yourself on the right course. Then: much learning, a skill or craft, being well trained, and speech that is well spoken.

That's the highest blessing. The poem keeps going, verse after verse, and the tradition counts thirty-eight blessings in all. Each verse ends with the same line, which works like a stamp: this is the highest blessing.
Here's what makes it different from lucky socks. An omen happens to you. These blessings are things you can do.
Choose your company. Learn something well. Speak well.
Fortune, in this poem, isn't waiting outside your door.
It's built into how you live. Tomorrow, the poem comes home: to parents, family and work.

how: The Mangala Sutta is among the most widely chanted protective texts in Theravada Buddhism; it is recited at weddings, house blessings and new beginnings, and many children learn it by heart.

o: a vow made before a journey
a temple bell rung at festivals

games.q: the highest blessings: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha's first blessing is about the company you keep
not associating with fools, associating with the wise, honoring the worthy.
the Mangala Sutta lists lucky omens to watch for
it answers with blessings you can do: wise company, learning, skill, good speech.
each verse ends with the same line

games.q: you're the god sent to ask the Buddha what the highest blessing is. what's the first thing he names?
o: seeing a white bird at dawn.
not keeping company with fools, but with the wise.
games.why: he begins with company: avoid fools, keep company with the wise, honor those worthy of honor.

practice: Bring to mind the people you spend the most time with, in person and on your screen, and notice, without judging, who leaves you a little wiser, kinder, steadier, and who leaves you a little worse.
Then let one wise person come to mind whose company you'd like more of, and hold them there for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Mangala. A blessing, good fortune: and in the Buddha's answer, not an omen but a way of living, starting with wise company. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit mangala: auspicious, a blessing or good omen. the name of Sn 2.4.

carryVoice: Your line: choose your company. Fortune you build, not fortune you wait for. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 2.4, Mangala Sutta, verses 1–4 (also Khuddakapatha 5)
Commentary on the Mangala Sutta: the debate over omens (seen, heard, sensed)
